settings.editor:
Carbon monoxide is one of the most serious safety concerns associated with gas heating systems. The gas is colorless and odorless, which means it can build up inside a home without being immediately noticed. If a furnace develops problems such as a cracked heat exchanger, blocked flue pipe, or improper combustion, carbon monoxide can leak into the air circulating through your forced air system.

For homeowners in the Tri-cities, furnaces operate frequently during colder months. That makes furnace safety and proper maintenance essential.

The good news is that homeowners can watch for several warning signs that may indicate a potential carbon monoxide problem. Understanding these signs can help you identify issues early and schedule a professional furnace inspection before the situation becomes dangerous.

settings.title: Quick Answer: How to Check Your Furnace for Carbon Monoxide

settings.editor: You can check for early signs of carbon monoxide from furnaces by monitoring carbon monoxide detectors, observing furnace flame color, inspecting for soot around the furnace, and watching for symptoms such as headaches or dizziness at home. A yellow pilot light, blocked venting pipes, or unusual furnace exhaust can indicate combustion problems. Routine furnace inspections and HVAC safety checks help ensure combustion gases vent safely outside.

settings.title: What Causes Carbon Monoxide from a Furnace?

settings.editor:
Carbon monoxide forms whenever fuel burns. In a properly operating gas furnace, combustion gases are safely vented outside through the furnace exhaust and flue system.

Problems occur when the system cannot vent gases properly or when furnace components become damaged.

Common causes include:

  • Cracked heat exchanger
  • Heat exchanger leak
  • Cracked firebox
  • Venting pipe blockage
  • Poor chimney draft
  • Improper burner combustion

When these problems occur, carbon monoxide can enter the air moving through your heating system vents.

settings.title: Signs of Carbon Monoxide from Furnace Systems

settings.editor: Homeowners cannot see carbon monoxide itself, but several warning signs may indicate a problem.

A properly functioning furnace produces a steady blue burner flame.
If the flame appears yellow or flickers, it may indicate incomplete combustion.

Warning signs include:

  • Yellow pilot light
  • Pilot light flickering
  • Uneven burner flames
  • Orange colored flame


Changes in furnace flame color often indicate combustion problems that should be evaluated during a furnace inspection.

settings.title: 2. Soot or Rust Around the Furnace

settings.editor:
Visual clues around the furnace can also indicate problems.

Look for:

  • Soot around furnace panels
  • Black residue near burners
  • Furnace rust around the combustion chamber
  • Discoloration near the vent system

Soot buildup suggests improper combustion. Rust may indicate moisture damage that can lead to a heat exchanger leak.
Both signs require a professional HVAC safety check.

Your furnace relies on proper ventilation to remove combustion gases.

A flue pipe inspection may reveal problems such as:

  • Disconnected vent pipes
  • Corrosion in the vent system
  • Venting pipe blockage from debris
  • Restricted chimney airflow


If combustion gases cannot escape properly, carbon monoxide may accumulate indoors.

Carbon monoxide symptoms can sometimes be the first warning sign.

Common symptoms include:

  • Headache at home
  • Nausea or fatigue
  • Dizziness
  • Feeling dizzy from furnace operation
  • Confusion or trouble concentrating

If these symptoms appear when the heating system is running and improve when leaving the house, carbon monoxide exposure may be possible.
Carbon monoxide poisoning can become dangerous quickly, so these symptoms should never be ignored.

Certain internal furnace problems increase carbon monoxide risk.

These include:

  • Cracked heat exchanger
  • Damaged firebox
  • Burner misalignment
  • Combustion airflow problems


The heat exchanger separates combustion gases from the air circulating through the home. When the exchanger cracks, carbon monoxide can enter the air supply.
Because these issues are difficult to see, professional furnace maintenance is critical.

settings.title: The Importance of Carbon Monoxide Detectors

settings.editor:
A carbon monoxide detector or CO alarm provides an essential layer of protection.

These devices monitor indoor air and alert homeowners when carbon monoxide levels rise.

Recommended installation locations include:

  • Outside sleeping areas
  • Near bedrooms
  • On each floor of the home
    Near heating equipment

Some homeowners also use an air quality monitor that measures carbon monoxide levels along with other pollutants.

Homeowners can look for warning signs, but a professional HVAC inspection provides the most reliable protection.

During furnace maintenance, an HVAC professional may perform:

  • Heat exchanger inspection
  • Flue pipe inspection
  • Combustion testing
  • Furnace exhaust evaluation
  • Airflow testing in the forced air system
  • Inspection of heating system vents

These checks help detect problems such as heat exchanger leaks, gas leak signs, or combustion issues before they become serious safety hazards.

settings.title: Frequently Asked Questions About Carbon Monoxide in Furnaces

items.item_title: Can carbon monoxide come from a furnace that still heats normally?
How often should carbon monoxide detectors be tested?
Can blocked vents cause carbon monoxide buildup?
Are boilers also at risk for carbon monoxide leaks?
What should I do if I suspect carbon monoxide in my home?

settings.editor: Yes. A furnace may continue heating normally even if a small heat exchanger crack or venting problem allows carbon monoxide to leak.
Carbon monoxide detectors should be tested monthly and batteries should be replaced at least once per year.
Yes. Venting pipe blockage or poor chimney draft can prevent combustion gases from exiting the home properly.
Yes. Boiler safety is important because boilers also burn fuel and produce combustion gases that must be vented properly.
Leave the home immediately, get fresh air, and contact emergency services if symptoms are present. The heating system should not be used again until an HVAC professional performs a full inspection.

settings.title: Stay Safe with Regular Furnace Safety Checks

settings.editor:
Carbon monoxide is a serious safety hazard, but many furnace problems show warning signs before they become dangerous. Watching for changes in furnace flame color, soot buildup, blocked vent pipes, and unusual health symptoms can help homeowners detect issues early.

Because carbon monoxide is invisible and odorless, regular furnace maintenance and working carbon monoxide detectors are the best ways to protect your household.
